task: This is a synthetic newspaper-writing exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes. Write from the reporting snapshot as of August 19, 2026. Write a headline and a 450–650-word AP-style news update about Merefold Dairy Cooperative's temporary powder-line shutdown, explaining the implications for employees and member farms.

facts.text: Merefold Dairy Cooperative announced Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, that it will suspend milk-powder production for nine months beginning Oct. 1.
The cooperative's fresh-milk packaging and cultured-products lines will continue operating.
Powder inventory stands at 3,600 tons, compared with 1,900 tons a year earlier, according to the cooperative's monthly stock report.
Chief executive Olin Wray said powder orders have fallen while storage and financing costs have increased.
The cooperative has not published customer-level order figures or attributed the change to a single buyer or trade measure.
The powder line has 42 employees: 22 will receive transfer offers to fresh products, 12 maintenance assignments and eight redundancy notices.
The wider plant employs 110 people, including the 42 assigned to the powder line.
Transfer offers preserve base pay but involve different shift times; acceptance totals are not yet available.
The cooperative will retain all contracted milk-collection volumes from its 87 member farms through the current contract year.
Some collected milk will be processed under a tolling agreement at Larkspur Dairies, 76 miles away.
The additional transport and tolling costs have not been disclosed, and next year's farm payment formula remains under review.
Member farmer Ina Selk said she needs the next payment schedule before renewing a feed contract.
Selk said, "Collecting the milk answers one question. What comes back on the statement answers another."
Employee representative Tavren Cole has asked the cooperative to offer retraining to the eight workers receiving redundancy notices.
No retraining agreement or severance total has been announced.
Wray said, "We are pausing one way of processing milk, not telling our farms to stop producing it."
The cooperative will reassess powder stocks and orders in March 2027 before committing to a restart date.
The nine-month planning period is not a guaranteed production restart, according to the board's notice.
The cooperative was formed by 19 farms in 1978 and added powder production in 2006.
The stock report supplies no evidence of milk being discarded or of a consumer shortage of fresh dairy products.
